annotations.text:
Cooking progress is stored on the phone,
so kitchen wifi dropping cannot
interrupt a cook.

A finished cook is the one thing that
queues when offline -- history is
append-only, so nothing can conflict.

Provider buttons are drawn plain here.
Real ones must follow Google's and
Apple's branding rules -- the one place
the design system does not win.

Creating is four pages so nothing is
overwhelming, and each saves the draft
as you go.

Editing is NOT. Fixing one wrong
quantity should not walk you through
four pages.

Ingredients and equipment each carry
a note: "carrots, not too long",
"roasting tin, at least 30 cm".

It goes in its own field, never the
name -- otherwise the shopping list
reads badly and the same ingredient
looks like three.

Nesting is the whole idea.
Indented steps happen DURING the
step above them.

One parentStepId reads three ways:
a drag handle when writing, a bracket
when reading, a "meanwhile" list
when cooking.

The app never opens the link.
The user's own AI watches the video.

The prompt is the hard part: it has to
teach a stranger's model what nesting
is, or imports come back flat.

Cook mode is used with wet hands,
from arm's length, knife in the other
hand.

Targets far above the 44pt minimum,
no audio in either direction, and none
of it is a mode -- nobody switches on
"dirty hands" once their hands are
dirty.

The photo is behind a button, never
inline.

An inline picture pushes the instruction
off a screen that needs big text. One
big tap to see it, one big tap to close.

Eleven tables, created in one migration
by 0001 so no later spec has to alter
a table that already holds data.

Two things worth arguing about:

steps.parentStepId is a tree, not a
graph -- one level, no cycles possible,
no edge table.

cooks.excluded stores NAMES, not ids.
History records what happened and
must not change when the recipe is
edited later.
